an0795.user: Quick one on my eyewear Google Search account — why is my CTR low? It's been sliding for about 6 weeks now. Same ads, same audience, nothing I changed. AOV is ₹2350, 60% margin. CAC has gone from ₹549 six weeks ago to ₹1189 now, ROAS dropped 4.3 to 2.0.
an0795.assistant:
Your CTR isn't the disease — it's a symptom, and the chart you should be staring at is frequency, sitting at 2.9. Above ~2.5 the same people are seeing the same ad for the third and fourth time, they've already decided, and they scroll past. That's why clicks soften, CAC more than doubles (₹549 to ₹1189), and ROAS halves. Same creatives, same audience, six straight weeks down: that's the textbook signature of creative fatigue, not a broken algorithm or bad targeting.

The economics aren't dead yet — contribution is ₹2350 × 60% − ₹1189 = +₹221 per order, so you're still making money, just thinner than six weeks ago. But the trend line is what kills you if you do nothing.

The lever: new creative angles, not a tweak to the existing ones. Different hook, different problem framing, fresh thumbnails — give the same audience a reason to look again. And build a testing cadence so you're never riding one winner until it collapses; you should always have the next angle warming up.

Caveat: refresh the creative before you touch budget or bids. If you cut spend now you'll just confirm a decline you could have reversed.

an0796.user: Bit worried about my candle store on Amazon Ads. CAC jumped 22% this week versus last week — that's a big move. We did 90 conversions this week. I'm thinking of overhauling the whole strategy, new keywords, new targeting, the works. Should I?
an0796.assistant:
Don't touch anything. A 22% CAC move on 90 conversions is well inside normal week-to-week variance — at that sample size a handful of orders landing on Monday instead of Sunday swings the number this much. There's no signal here to act on.

The real risk isn't the CAC bump; it's you. Overhauling a working account off one noisy week is how founders whipsaw themselves into a worse position than the noise ever cost them.

What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band. Until then, leave it running and watch.

an0797.user: New to reading these dashboards — why is my CTR low at 1.9%? Logistics SaaS, last 30 days: AOV ₹1250, margin 57%, CAC ₹349, ROAS 3.6, and 90-day repeat is sitting at 10%.
an0797.assistant:
1.9% CTR is fine — that's a normal number, stop staring at it. Look downstream, because your acquisition is genuinely working: contribution on the first order is ₹1250 × 57% − ₹349 = +₹364, and a 3.6 ROAS confirms the front of the funnel is healthy.

The number that should worry you is 90-day repeat at 10%. With barely anyone coming back for a second order, your LTV is basically just that first purchase — and once you start scaling spend, CAC rises and that thin first-order margin gets squeezed with no repeat revenue to catch you. You're filling a bucket with no bottom.

Fix repeat before you scale. Figure out why 9 in 10 customers don't return — onboarding, the second-purchase trigger, whatever your renewal moment is — and plug that leak first. The ads aren't the problem; the lack of a back end is.

Caveat: 10% over 90 days is a snapshot; check whether your sales cycle is just longer than 90 days before you conclude it's pure churn.

an0798.user: Want the non-obvious read here. Haircare brand, organic/SEO traffic. Over the last 6 weeks CAC has crept from ₹334 to ₹626 and ROAS slid 4.6 to 2.5. AOV ₹1550, 60% margin, frequency 3.8. CTR's been sliding too. I haven't changed the content or the audience.
an0798.assistant:
The non-obvious part is that this isn't an SEO or audience problem at all, even though nothing's broken on those fronts. Frequency at 3.8 is the tell — the same people are hitting the same content nearly four times, well past the ~2.5 mark where attention drops off. CTR slides, CAC nearly doubles (₹334 to ₹626), ROAS halves. Unchanged creative plus unchanged audience over six weeks is creative fatigue, full stop.

You're still in the black — contribution is ₹1550 × 60% − ₹626 = +₹304 per order — so this is a fix-it-before-it-worsens situation, not an emergency. But the trajectory is the warning.

The move: rotate in genuinely new angles, not cosmetic edits to what you have. Same audience needs a fresh reason to engage. And put a testing cadence in place so a new angle is always queued — that's how you stop riding one winner into the ground.

Caveat: confirm the frequency reading is over a sensible window; a 3.8 averaged over six weeks behaves differently than 3.8 in the last seven days, and it changes how fast you need to move.

an0799.user: My CAC is killing me on Performance Max — Meesho seller, AOV ₹1300, CAC ₹530, ROAS 2.5, CTR 1.7%. How do I lower my CAC? Feels like the targeting is off or Google's just burning my money.
an0799.assistant:
You're chasing the wrong number. Run the contribution: ₹1300 × 24% − ₹530 = −₹218 per order. You lose money on every sale, and that's not because of CAC — it's because your gross margin is 24%. Even if you got CAC down to ₹300, ₹312 of margin minus ₹300 leaves you ₹12 a unit, working flat out to go nowhere.

This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. No targeting tweak, no negative keyword, no bid strategy fixes a 24% margin — the maths simply doesn't allow profitable acquisition at that level. A 2.5 ROAS that looks borderline-okay is hiding the fact that you can't afford to advertise at all yet.

The lever is COGS, pricing, and AOV — not the ad account. Negotiate cost down, raise price where the category lets you, or bundle to push AOV up so the percentage margin actually covers a paid customer. Get margin north of where ₹1300 × margin clears ₹530-plus-profit, then come back to scaling ads.

Caveat: if 24% is post-Meesho-commission, the real product margin might be healthier — worth separating platform fees from true COGS before you reprice.

an0800.user: Coffee brand here, running WhatsApp broadcast traffic to the site. Over the last 30 days we pushed out a lot — about 1.36 million impressions, got 22,748 clicks, so CTR around 1.7%. But only 254 orders, conversion rate just 1.12%. AOV ₹950. We're on broad-match keywords. The reach feels great so I'm confused why sales aren't following.
an0800.assistant:
The reach is exactly the problem, not the consolation. 1.36M impressions and 22.7K clicks look like momentum, but a 1.12% conversion rate is the number that tells the real story: you're buying enormous volumes of low-intent traffic. Broad-match is pulling in people who are curious, comparison-browsing, or clicked by accident — not people in the market for coffee right now.

Your CTR of 1.7% is perfectly normal; clicks were never the issue. The funnel breaks at intent. When traffic is broad, the click is cheap but the buyer isn't there, so 22,748 clicks limp to just 254 orders.

The lever: tighten to high-intent. Move off broad-match onto phrase/exact for the terms that signal purchase intent, pile in negative keywords to cut the browsers, and stop letting the system optimise toward clicks — optimise toward purchases. You'll buy fewer, more expensive clicks that actually convert.

Caveat: as you narrow, volume will drop and your cost-per-click will rise — that's expected and fine, because you're trading junk reach for orders. Judge the change on conversion rate and contribution, not on the impression count falling.

an0801.user: Okay I'm a bit panicked — kids-coding edtech, I put ₹35K into Google Search over the last 6 days and got 15 conversions. Is my CAC good?? Should I scale this hard or kill it before I waste more money? I keep doing the math and freaking out.
an0801.assistant:
Stop doing the math — there isn't enough of it to mean anything yet. 15 conversions over 6 days is far too small a sample to judge CAC, ROAS or anything else; one good day or one dud day moves your number by 30-40%. Any conclusion you draw right now is noise, and both 'scale hard' and 'kill it' would be guesses dressed up as decisions.

The honest answer is: we can't know yet. Let it run until you have roughly 100 conversions, or a clean 2-3 week window, whichever comes first. That's the threshold where CAC stabilises enough to trust.

Until then, hold the budget steady and resist the urge to touch it. Reacting to 15 data points is how you talk yourself out of a campaign that was actually fine.

an0802.user: HR-tech SaaS. Last 90 days we're doing ₹23L/month, unit economics look healthy. Channel mix: Google Search is about 97% of revenue, everything else maybe 3%. Pasting it as-is — what's wrong? Honestly it all looks good to me.
an0802.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with the numbers — the unit economics are fine, the revenue's real. What's wrong is the shape of the risk underneath them. 97% of a ₹23L/month business rides on a single channel. That's not a performance problem; it's a concentration problem.

Think about what 97% means in practice: one Google algorithm update, one ad-account suspension, one CPC spike in your category, and your revenue doesn't dip — it halves overnight, with no second engine to catch the fall. Healthy unit economics on a single channel is a strong business standing on one leg.

The move isn't to fix anything in the account — it's to start a genuine second channel now, while it's a calm strategic choice and not an emergency scramble. LinkedIn for HR-tech, outbound, content/SEO, a partnership motion — pick one and give it real budget and a real quarter, not a token test.

Caveat: don't yank spend off Google to fund it — it's working. Build the second channel alongside, and measure it on its own CAC, expecting it to look worse than Google at first because Google is mature and this one's newborn.

an0803.user: Flipkart seller, Performance Max. AOV ₹1450, CAC ₹745, ROAS 1.9, CTR 1.7%. My CAC is way too high — how do I bring it down? I've tried audiences, bids, everything and it won't budge.
an0803.assistant:
Before you touch CAC again, look at what a sale actually earns you: ₹1450 × 32% − ₹745 = −₹281 per order. You're underwater on every unit sold, and CAC isn't the cause — a 32% gross margin is. That's the disease; the ad cost is just where it shows up.

Here's why no bid or audience change will save it: at 32% margin, each order generates ₹464 of gross profit. To break even your CAC has to sit below ₹464 — and you'd still make nothing. To make real money you'd need CAC in the ₹250-300 range, which is a different universe from ₹745. You can't optimise your way across that gap; the margin simply doesn't fund a paid customer.

This is a margin problem in a marketing costume. The lever is COGS, pricing and AOV — cut product cost, raise price where Flipkart's category lets you, or bundle to lift the order value so the percentage clears a customer with profit to spare. Fix that, then the ads become worth scaling.

Caveat: check whether that 32% is before or after Flipkart commission and fees — if it's after, your true product margin may be more workable than it looks, and the repricing job is smaller.

an0804.user: Honestly stressing about this — eyewear brand, spent ₹3L on email-driven campaigns last 30 days, ROAS only 1.7. That feels terrible right? AOV ₹2450, 68% margin, CAC ₹1438, CTR 1.7%, repeat at 39%. Do I cut this before it bleeds more?
an0804.assistant:
Breathe — you're reading the wrong number and scaring yourself with it. ROAS of 1.7 looks weak only if you ignore your margin. Run the real figure: contribution is ₹2450 × 68% − ₹1438 = +₹228 per order. That's genuinely profitable on the first sale, before a single repeat purchase.

And your repeat is 39% over 90 days — solid. So every cohort you acquire isn't just clearing +₹228 once; a healthy chunk comes back and buys again, stacking margin on top of an already-positive first order. ROAS is a vanity metric that doesn't know your 68% margin exists; contribution does, and contribution says this account is winning.

This shouldn't be cut — it should be scaling. The lever is to stop judging on ROAS entirely and push more budget while contribution stays positive, watching CAC as you scale.

Caveat: as you increase spend, CAC will drift up from ₹1438 — keep an eye on the point where ₹1666 of gross margin stops covering it. That's your real ceiling, not the ROAS number.

an0805.user: Gym, email channel, last 30 days. Dropping the numbers: AOV ₹1450, margin 45%, CAC ₹444, ROAS 3.3, CTR 1.7%, 90-day repeat 10%. What's wrong? On paper it looks like it's working.
an0805.assistant:
On the front end it is working — that's the trap. Contribution on the first sale is ₹1450 × 45% − ₹444 = +₹208 per member, and a 3.3 ROAS confirms acquisition is doing its job. If you only look here, you scale and feel smart.

The leak is one number: 90-day repeat at 10%. For a gym, that's brutal — you're acquiring members who pay once and vanish, so your LTV is basically that single ₹208 contribution and nothing behind it. The whole model of a gym is retention; 10% means people sign up and don't come back, which means the second payment never lands.

Don't scale spend into that. The lever is fixing repeat first — onboarding the first 30 days, attendance habit, the renewal nudge — because pouring more CAC into a 10%-retention funnel just buys you more one-time members and a faster bleed.

Caveat: confirm whether '90-day repeat' is capturing membership renewals or only repeat transactions — if it's the latter and most revenue is a recurring plan, the picture's less grim and you'd measure churn instead.

an0806.user: Panicking a little — dental clinic, running WhatsApp broadcasts. Last 30 days AOV ₹1450, margin 48%, CAC ₹416, ROAS 3.5, CTR 1.4%, but my 90-day repeat is only 8%. The ROAS looks fine so why does it feel like I'm not growing?
an0806.assistant:
Your instinct is right and the ROAS is lying to you by omission. Acquisition is genuinely healthy — contribution on the first visit is ₹1450 × 48% − ₹416 = +₹280 per patient, and 3.5 ROAS backs that up. The CTR of 1.4% is normal, nothing to fix there.

The reason it feels like you're running to stand still is the 8% 90-day repeat. A dental clinic lives on patients coming back — cleanings, follow-ups, the next family member — and 92% never returning means you're constantly buying brand-new patients just to replace the ones who didn't come back. That's expensive growth that doesn't compound.

Fix retention before you spend a rupee more on acquisition. The lever: a recall system — WhatsApp reminders for the 6-month checkup, a follow-up after every treatment, a reason to return — so each patient is worth more than one ₹280 visit. Right now you're filling a bucket with no bottom.

Caveat: 90 days may be too short a window for a dental recall cycle, which often runs 6 months — pull a 6-month repeat number before you decide how bad the leak really is.

an0807.user: IELTS edtech, running Meesho Ads. Let me describe it — last 30 days we had about 20,000 visits, 1,368 added to cart, 796 got to checkout, and 223 actually bought. CTR's around 1.7%. I'm new to this, not sure where the problem is.
an0807.assistant:
Walk the funnel and the leak points to itself. 20,000 visits to 1,368 add-to-cart is a ~7% ATC rate — that's healthy; your ads and product page are doing their job. 1,368 down to 796 reaching checkout is normal browsing drop-off. The break is the last step: 796 reached checkout, only 223 bought. That's a 28% checkout-to-purchase rate, when a working checkout should land somewhere around 50-70%.

So this isn't an acquisition or traffic problem — the money you're spending to bring people in is fine. People are showing up at the till with their wallet out and something is stopping them. That's checkout friction: surprise shipping or fees appearing at the end, a forced account login, or missing payment options like UPI or COD that Indian buyers expect.

The lever: instrument that final step and fix it. Add the checkout events so you can see exactly where the 573 people drop, then remove the friction — show shipping up front, allow guest checkout, turn on UPI and COD. Recovering even half of that drop roughly doubles your orders with zero extra ad spend.

Caveat: 223 purchases is a usable sample but watch it over another few weeks once you instrument — make sure 28% is the steady rate and not one bad fortnight.

an0808.user: Haircare brand, Google Search, ₹6.5L spend last 30 days, post-iOS. Here's my headache — Meta-side the platform says 3.6 ROAS, but Shopify last-click shows 1.6. The two dashboards completely disagree and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. Which do I believe?
an0808.assistant:
Neither, as an absolute — and that's the answer, not a dodge. Platform-reported 3.6 is modelled conversions on a 7-day-click window; the platform is grading its own homework and leans generous. Shopify last-click at 1.6 only credits the final touch and ignores every assist the ads gave along the way, so it leans stingy. Both are biased in opposite directions; the truth sits somewhere between them, and refereeing the two will never resolve because they're measuring different things.

Stop trying to pick a winner between two dashboards that are structurally built to disagree. The number you can actually trust is blended CAC: total spend ÷ actual new customers. On ₹6.5L, count the genuinely new customers Shopify recorded this period, divide, and you get one real, channel-agnostic cost you can manage to — no attribution model required.

The lever: anchor every decision on blended CAC against your contribution per order, and treat platform ROAS as a directional signal for which creative is working, not as financial truth.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs channels together, so if you're scaling more than one at once you'll need a holdout or geo-test to know what's incremental — but it's still a far more honest north star than either dashboard alone.
